newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end with hefty losses, financials weak.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end with hefty losses, financials weak.

text.p: Tokyo stocks ended Wednesday trade with hefty losses brought on by continued selling of financial sector shares and profit-taking of some bellwether issues which had rallied on Tuesday, brokers said.
The 225-share Nikkei average finished 318.33 points or 1.77 percent lower at 17,703.37. Its June futures shed 330 points to close at 17,710.

"The basic trend remains unchanged," said Kunihiro Hatae, general manager at Tokyo Securities Co Ltd. "Banks, brokerages and construction sectors were being sold and some export-strong shares, encouraged by the weak yen, were bought."
Losers ballooned to 940 while only 197 issues advanced. There were 107 issues unchanged. A total of 423 million shares changed hands, down from 477 million the previous day.

The TOPIX index fell 21.66 points or 1.59 percent to 1,343.39. The Nikkei 300 fell 4.12 points or 1.55 percent to 260.95. The second section index slipped 20.73 points or 1.31 percent to 1,562.14. Second-section turnover was 8.93 million shares, slightly up from 7.78 million on Tuesday.
The Nikkei benchmark stayed in negative territory for the whole day, buckling under the weight of profit-taking, following a rise of over 300 points in the previous session.

Indices slid further in the afternoon session, after selling of futures was sparked off partly by comments from a government official that a review of the securities transaction tax would carried out together with a review of the capital gains tax.
Some issues in sectors strapped with bad loans drooped to new lows for the 1997 calendar year. Daiwa Securities Co Ltd was down 30 yen at 715, and Wako Securities Co Ltd lost 36 yen to 429.
Daiwa Bank Ltd slipped 15 yen to 341 and Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd fell six yen to 135.

"Sell orders coming from elimination of cross shareholdings as well as porfolio reshuffling are sending some issues in the sector to new lows, day after day," a broker at a middle-sized brokerage said.

Brokers said that although there was some profit-taking of blue-chip issues such as Sony Corp, which lost 20 yen to end at 9,100, other stocks were bought and prevented the Nikkei average from plunging further.
Fujitsu Ltd added 10 yen to 1,300 in trade of 5.49 million shares, making it the fifth most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse.
Sharp Corp climbed 40 yen to 1,540 and Canon Inc rose 10 yen to 2,940.
"Technically, blue chips are ready for a breather, but institutional investors are racing to include high performers in their portfolios and the buying is not stopping," a "Big Four" trader said.

Brokers said that as long as the yen remained weak, but not excessively so, it would make exporters attractive to investors. The yen weakened to about 126.64/74 late on Wednesday. It had stood at around 125.80/90 in late Tokyo on Tuesday.

Brokers said market participants were watching carefully to see whether a large differential between U.S. and Japanese interest rates and the dollar's continuing surge against the yen would accelerate an outflow of capital from Japan.

"Japanese financial institutions are not making full-fledged attempts to buy stocks yet," Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, was quoted as saying in Wednesday's Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper that a vast amount of money is now in Japan, and though some is being used to buy Japanese bonds, some is flowing out of Japan, causing the depreciation of the yen.
Nintendo Co Ltd shares surged 180 yen to 9,300 on hopes that the Osaka bourse will start options transactions and that options in Nintendo will be among those traded.

Yamanouchi Pharmaceutical Co Ltd climbed 10 yen to 2,570 on a bright business forecast for 1997/98. Apparel retailer Suzutan Co Ltd tumbled 28 yen to 164, a record low, after Japan's securities watchdog said it suspected former executives of insider trading, brokers said.
The only sector with major gains was automobiles. Warehouses, securities, banks, land transport and mining were the main retreaters.
--Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk
